understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call feeling cut off, and that is where this week begins.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the waiting as real, and the love behind it, without blame.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the waiting is for a future that will not arrive, and that is what keeps the heart from settling.
week_beats.steady: You hold that what is real in you cannot be lost, and the love is yours regardless of distance.
week_beats.act: You try letting the mind rest in what is real now, and finding one small thing to do that belongs to this day.
week_beats.story: A mother who waited for a son who would not return shows you what love looks like when it no longer asks for anything back.

queries.hook: The waiting that will not stop, and the heart that cannot be taught to let go; the gap between the life you built and the one that will not come back.
queries.diagnose: When the mind waits for a future that will not arrive, it exhausts itself; the waiting is not your fault, but it is what keeps the heart from settling.
queries.steady: What is real in you cannot be lost; the love you have is yours, and it does not depend on the distance between you.
queries.act: Let the mind rest in what is real now; speak the true thing to your heart, and find one small thing to do that belongs to this day, not to the waiting.
queries.story: A mother who waited for a son who would not return, and found, in the waiting itself, a different kind of love that did not ask for anything back.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

matched.label: I can't focus, my mind is restless

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna stands in the middle of the battlefield and tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees. He says the mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.
verse.for_you: The waiting you sit with every day is the wind. It does not ask your permission to blow, and it does not stop because you wish it to. The practice is not to pin the wind down.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse.sanskrit: ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते । सङ्गात् संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
verse.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.
verse.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

prasang.title: The person of steady wisdom
prasang.summary: Arjuna asks how a steady person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna describes someone content within, unshaken by sorrow, master of the senses, and traces how dwelling on things leads to anger and ruin.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

verse.meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna's question about the steady mind. He says when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire comes anger. He traces how guarding attention keeps a person whole.
verse.for_you: Yesterday's verse named the grip. Today the Gita names the pattern. The waiting is a desire for a future that will not arrive. The anger is the grief of knowing that. Your attention is the gate. You do not need to stop the feeling.

verse.speaker: Rahim
verse.setting: Rahim on a love so close it needs no news.
verse.sanskrit: जेहिं रहीम तन-मन दियो, कियो हिए बिच भौन। तासों दुख-सुख कहन की, रही बात अब कौन॥
verse.line: The one who lives in your heart already knows your joys and sorrows. Nothing needs explaining.
verse.translation: Rahim says: to the one who has been given body and mind, who has made a home in the heart, what joy or sorrow is left that needs telling?
verse.for_you: Rahim says the one who lives in your heart already knows your joys and sorrows. The love you have for your son is not a message that needs a reply. It is the air you breathe.

verse.speaker: Rahim
verse.sanskrit: रहिमन सुधि सबते भली, लगै जो बारम्बार। बिछुरे मानुष फिरि मिलैं, यहै जानि अवतार॥
verse.line: Remembering is a kind of nearness. People who were parted do meet again.
verse.translation: Rahim says: remembering is best of all, when it comes again and again. People who were separated meet again; know that this is why God takes birth.

matched.label: My parents are getting older far away

verse.meaning: Rahim tells the reader that remembering is a kind of nearness. When it comes again and again, it keeps people who were separated in touch. He says the separated meet again, and God takes birth just to make this happen. The verse suggests that the love you carry is already here, in the act of calling it to mind. It does not ask you to wait for a return, but to hold the connection alive right where you are.
verse.for_you: The love for your son is not in the waiting room. It lives in the memories you bring up in these long hours. Let that remembrance be the nearness you feel today.

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Follows the call to enjoy by letting go: how to live and work.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वन्नेवेह कर्माणि जिजीविषेच्छतꣳ समाः । एवं त्वयि नान्यथेतोऽस्ति न कर्म लिप्यते नरे ॥
verse.line: Do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling.
verse.translation: Doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.why: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

prasang.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

verse.meaning: The Seer tells the reader to do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling. The verse proposes that you keep working and living fully, but without letting your actions stick to you. You can wish for a long life and do your tasks without letting them hold you hostage.
verse.for_you: Today, try doing one small task from your morning routine and let it go when it is done. Let your mind rest in the doing, not in the waiting.

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: The sage Vasishtha to Bharat, shattered by his father's death and Ram's exile.
verse.sanskrit: तात हृदयँ धीरजु धरहु करहु जो अवसर आजु। उठे भरत गुर बचन सुनि करन कहेउ सबु साजु ॥
verse.line: Keep courage in your heart, and do what today asks of you.
verse.translation: "Child, keep courage in your heart, and do what this moment asks of you today." Hearing his teacher, Bharat rose and had everything made ready.
verse.why: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

prasang.title: Bharat refuses the throne
prasang.summary: After the funeral, Vasishtha, the ministers and Kausalya all urge Bharat to rule, as his father wished. Bharat says the advice is right and his heart still isn't at peace; the crown means nothing without Ram. He decides to go to the forest, admit his fault, and trust his brother to forgive.
prasang.story_hook: Everyone agreed the throne was his, and Bharat could not bring himself to sit on it.
prasang.lesson: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha, the king's wise brother, speaks to Bharat, a young prince broken by grief and guilt over his father's death and his brother Ram's exile. Bharat has refused the throne, and the sage urges him to find courage in his heart and do what the present moment asks of him. The verse proposes that when the mind is torn between what was and what should be, the only way forward is to act on the truth of the current moment.
verse.for_you: Today, answer the call of this morning. Make your tea, water your plants, or sit with a book. Do what this moment asks of you.

story.title: Shabari's long wait
story.story_hook: Her teachers had all gone, and still she gathered fruit every day for a guest who had never come.
story.summary: The old ascetic woman Shabari has lived for years at Pampa after her teachers died, told that Ram would one day come. She has kept gathering forest food for him. When he arrives, she welcomes him, shows him her teachers' forest, and departs in peace.
story.lesson: Faithful waiting, unseen by the world, is not wasted.

anchor.speaker: Shabari
anchor.setting: The old ascetic woman Shabari has waited years at Pampa for Ram, as her teachers foretold.
anchor.sanskrit: एवमुक्ता महाभागैस्तदाहं पुरुषर्षभ। मया तु संचितं वन्यं विविधं पुरुषर्षभ॥ तवार्थे पुरुषव्याघ्र पम्पायास्तीरसम्भवम्।
anchor.line: I was told you would come, so I kept gathering for you. Waiting was a kind of preparing.
anchor.translation: So the great ones told me, best of men, and for you I have gathered every kind of forest food from the banks of the Pampa.
anchor.why: Faithful waiting, unseen by the world, is not wasted.

prasang.summary: The old ascetic woman Shabari has lived for years at Pampa after her teachers died, told that Ram would one day come. She has kept gathering forest food for him. When he arrives, she welcomes him, shows him her teachers' forest, and departs in peace.
prasang.story_hook: Her teachers had all gone, and still she gathered fruit every day for a guest who had never come.

story.hook_title: Shabari, an old woman in the forest, gathered fruit every day for a guest who never came
story.teaser: Shabari, an old woman in the forest, gathered fruit every day for a guest who never came
story.for_you: Shabari gathered fruit long after her teachers were gone, for a guest who had not yet arrived. They did not need to see him to keep their hands busy. In your own quiet hours, let your waiting become a gathering of your own.

weeks.title: The waiting that will not stop

script: You are resting in a life that feels much smaller than the one you built. The hours stretch. You are waiting for a door that will not open. And the waiting has no end.
Arjuna stands in the middle of the battlefield. He tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. Arjuna said:
चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम्, तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम्.
In plain words: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.

The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it. This is easier said than done, because you cannot fight the wind. You can only learn to stand in it without being blown away. The practice is not to pin the wind down.
When you sit in the quiet after the morning tea, you do not have to hold the waiting. Just sit with it. Let it blow. Let it go.
Can you stand in the wind without fighting it?

depth.life: The hours on the phone stretch out. You sit with the waiting, the same space where your son used to be. The mind drifts to the past and the empty room, restless and without a shore.
depth.points: The mind is not an enemy to be fought. It is a force that moves on its own, and your part is to let it move without catching it.
depth.practice: Sit with the phone in your lap and watch the mind drift. Do not pull it back.
depth.question: What would it be like to let the wind blow?
